title: Psychological and physiological effects of soundscapes: A systematic review of 25 experiments in the English and Chinese literature
review_question: To investigate psychological and physiological responses to soundscapes, audio-visual interactions, and assess the risk of bias and research quality in soundscape research.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Included empirical, quantitative studies measuring both psychological and physiological responses to soundscapes. Excluded qualitative, review studies, pure music, religious sounds, humanistic sounds, historical sounds, medical research, and studies on material differences.

search_databases: National Digital Library of Theses and Dissertations in Taiwan

synthesis_conclusions: There are significant associations between psychological and physiological responses evoked by the acoustic environment.
Audio-visual interaction influences both psychological and physiological responses.
Interpretation of findings should be cautious due to the high risk of bias and low research quality of included studies.
The reviewed studies provide consistent evidence, and replications are critical for trustworthy results.
evidence_gaps: Limited studies, particularly in the Americas and Africa.
Need for more studies on how pleasant, mixed, and signal-to-noise ratio sounds improve psychophysiological well-being.
Lack of common ground for psychological response measurements; need to consolidate to key dimensions (pleasantness, preference, tranquility, ISO 12913-2:2018 semantic dimensions, 11 adjective pairs).
Need for more research on HRV and salivary analysis for physiological stress.
Need for more research on gender differences in soundscape effects.
Need for more research on the effect of compatibility and appropriateness of soundscapes.
Need for more research on the influence of human activity sounds on psychological and physiological responses.
Need for more research on the interaction between auditory and visual stimuli on psychological and physiological effects.
Need for integration of sensory modalities, environmental factors, contextual indicators, temporal data, demographic variables, and socio-cultural factors in soundscape research.
risk_of_bias_assessment: JBI Checklist for Randomized Controlled Trials was used. Average score for included studies was 24.00% (range 7.69% to 38.46%), indicating high risk of bias and low research quality.
heterogeneity_sources: Considerable diversity of psychological response types, making meta-analysis difficult.
publication_bias: Searched both English and Chinese journal articles and gray literature (theses, dissertations, conference papers) to reduce language and publication bias, but acknowledged a possibility of remaining language bias.

moderators.effect: Males showed more significant RR response to pleasant sounds and greater HR decrease to unpleasant sounds than females. Different flowing water sounds had greater tension/fatigue/annoyance reduction in males. Urban park soundscapes had greater restoration effect on girls. Fountain sounds had better EDA/HR restoration for boys.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Males: increased RR to pleasant sounds, decreased HR to unpleasant sounds, greater tension/fatigue/annoyance reduction from flowing water sounds. Females: less pronounced physiological responses. Girls: greater restoration from urban park soundscapes. Boys: better EDA/HR restoration from fountain sounds.

limitations: Possibility of remaining language bias despite searching English and Chinese databases.
Single reviewer (P.R.K.) conducted initial screening, extraction, and quality assessment, with cross-checking by K.T.H., which may influence correctness.
Low average research quality (24% JBI score) of included studies, warranting cautious interpretation.
High diversity of psychological response types made meta-analysis difficult.
